item.title: Jury Finds Man Guilty of Arson in Devastating L.A. Fire
item.description:
A jury in Los Angeles on Friday found a 30-year-old man guilty of arson charges for his role in igniting one of the most destructive wildfires in California history.

After deliberating for two days, the jury found that the man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, had used a lighter to start a brush fire on New Year’s morning in 2025 in a clearing on a hill above Pacific Palisades, a wealthy coastal neighborhood in Los Angeles.

That blaze, known as the Lachman fire, was seemingly extinguished by firefighters. But six days later, amid a fierce windstorm, embers that had been smoldering underground grew into the Palisades fire, which destroyed thousands of homes and killed 12 people.

It was the second time Mr. Rinderknecht was tried in federal court in connection with the blaze. His first trial, in June, ended in a mistrial after jurors said they could not reach consensus. In that trial, they deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal.

Federal prosecutors quickly vowed to try him again.

They decided to narrow their case, charging Mr. Rinderknecht with two arson-related felonies rather than the three he faced in his first trial. One of the charges focused solely on the Lachman fire — the first blaze, which was extinguished — meaning that in the second trial, jurors had the option of convicting him of arson even if they did not believe he should be held responsible for the Palisades fire.

The other arson charge was related to destruction of property used in interstate commerce — the fire burned in part on federal land — and was connected to both the Lachman and Palisades fires. The jury convicted Mr. Rinderknecht of both counts.

A federal investigation determined that the Palisades fire was started by the first fire, or holdover fire, and prosecutors argued that Mr. Rinderknecht started the initial fire, using a grill lighter.

Prosecutors also shifted their arguments for the second trial — opting not to assert that Mr. Rinderknecht was motivated by a resentment of the wealthy and that he had admired Luigi Mangione, the man who drew populist support after he was accused of murdering a health insurance executive on the streets of New York City.

Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer, Steven Haney, denied that his client was culpable, saying that the fire was likely ignited by fireworks set off by New Year’s Eve revelers. He argued to the jury that there was no direct evidence — either witnesses or surveillance camera footage — that showed his client lighting the fire.

He said that Mr. Rinderknecht had previously lived in the area, and that he had hiked up to the clearing to watch fireworks that night. Phone records showed that Mr. Rinderknecht had made many calls to 911, which Mr. Haney argued were efforts by a concerned citizen to alert the authorities about the blaze.

The trial lasted a little more than two weeks , and jurors deliberated for two days before reaching a verdict.

The prosecution argued that Mr. Rinderknecht, who was working as an Uber driver on Dec. 31, 2024, was angry and lonely because he had no New Year’s plans. They presented cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to place him on the scene.

“While people in the community celebrated New Year’s Eve, the defendant had other plans,” Mark Williams, an assistant U.S. attorney, told jurors during his closing argument.

Prosecutors said Mr. Rinderknecht called 911 after igniting the brush fire, and then drove away, passing firefighters who were on responding to the fire. He then turned around and followed the fire trucks back to the scene, prosecutors said, where he took videos of the firefighters on his iPhone and listened to a French rap song about despair.

Prosecutors also introduced a query Mr. Rinderknecht made to ChatGPT after he called 911: “are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?” Prosecutors suggested he was trying to establish that he had lit the fire unintentionally.

In the defense closing argument, Mr. Haney tried to steer the jury’s attention to what he portrayed as major lapses in the government’s case. He said prosecutors had settled first on the theory of how the fire started, charged his client next and then tested key evidence. He also argued that the scene, known as Buddha Hill, was left unprotected for 12 days. It took investigators that long to go to the scene and try to determine the cause of the Lachman fire, he said.

Mr. Haney also told the jury to ignore the fact that a lighter was found in Mr. Rinderknecht’s car, which the prosecution presented as evidence.

“It doesn’t prove anything about what happened at the top of Buddha Hill that night,” Mr. Haney said to the jury. “That’s not evidence of arson, that’s evidence of a smoker.”

At the time of the fire, Mr. Rinderknecht was living alone in an apartment in North Hollywood. He had lived an itinerant life, having grown up in France before later living in Michigan, Florida and California.

item.title: Bobby Ray Inman, Intelligence Official Under Carter and Reagan, Dies at 95
item.description:
Bobby Ray Inman, a senior intelligence official in the Carter and Reagan administrations who was later nominated by President Bill Clinton to be secretary of defense, only to startle Washington by withdrawing from consideration a month later, died on Thursday in Austin, Texas. He was 95.

The death, in a hospital, was confirmed by his son Thomas, who did not provide a cause.

An admiral who was the director of naval intelligence from 1974 to 1976 before entering government service, he was the archetype of the electronic-age spy, overseeing the uncovering of secrets through technological wizardry in contrast with the timeworn image of the shadowy trench coat agents engaged in intrigue on enemy soil.

President Jimmy Carter named Admiral Inman in July 1977 to serve as director of the supersecret National Security Agency, which was charged with eavesdropping on foreign communications, codebreaking and averting the penetration of American secrets and other sensitive information from abroad.

Having taken the post a year after a Senate committee found that the N.S.A. had improperly engaged in domestic surveillance, Admiral Inman supported the adoption of the 1978 Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which required the approval of a special court to intercept international communications involving anyone in the United States.

“I became convinced that for almost anything the country needed to do, you could get legislation to put it on a solid foundation,” he told The New York Times in 2006. “There was the comfort of going out and saying in speeches, ‘We don’t target U.S. citizens, and what we do is authorized by a court.’”

Admiral Inman also helped establish a voluntary system under which scientists publishing codemaking and codebreaking material submitted their research to the N.S.A. for clearance, to prevent the Soviet Union from obtaining such sensitive material.

He forged close ties with the press, and he won support from Senate and House committees through briefings that legislators regarded as knowledgeable, forthright and devoid of a political agenda.

“One of the things that’s always helped him is his willingness to admit things that may go against his department’s interests,” Senator Patrick Leahy, the Vermont Democrat who served as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee during Admiral Inman’s tenure at the agency, told The Times in 1993. “When he would disagree with me and he’d make his case, I felt I could believe what he was saying.”

Admiral Inman served as director of the N.S.A. until February 1981, when President Ronald Reagan, in his first full month in office, nominated him as deputy director of central intelligence under the newly installed director, William J. Casey, who had managed Reagan’s presidential campaign.

Admiral Inman played a critical role in planning a hugely expensive enhancement of C.I.A. surveillance capabilities. But his relationship with Mr. Casey was strained, and he fought to maintain controls on domestic intelligence-gathering that had been imposed by Presidents Carter and Gerald R. Ford. He resigned after 16 months, saying he was tired of “petty bureaucratic intrigue” and wanted to enter the business world.

After retiring as a four-star admiral, he advised a House intelligence panel, founded a consortium to spur technological research, served as chairman of a holding firm for military contractors and was chief of a Reagan administration commission on embassy security.

In mid-December 1993, President Clinton nominated Admiral Inman to succeed Les Aspin, a former congressman, as defense secretary. Administration officials cited his credibility with the military, his strong administrative skills and his ability to clearly articulate policy in public settings.

“I am an operator, hopefully with a strategic view,” Admiral Inman said.

A trim 6 feet 2 inches with a military brush cut, he was described by The Times as possessing a “gaptoothed smile and self-deprecating demeanor” that “conceal a steely center, an extraordinary intellect and a remarkable ability to shape quietly the opinions of other officials.”

But he seemed lukewarm about the prospect of running the Pentagon.

Standing alongside Mr. Clinton in the White House Rose Garden, he said that in order to accept the nomination, he had needed to attain a “level of comfort” with him. “I would tell you up front, honestly, I did not vote for President Clinton,” he said, referring to the 1992 presidential race, in which Mr. Clinton defeated President George H.W. Bush. “I voted for President Bush, even though I was mad at him about his handling of the economy, but because I considered him a personal friend.”

He said he had neither sought nor wanted the defense secretary’s post but had agreed to be nominated for considerations of “duty and country.”

Congressional hearings on Mr. Inman’s nomination were expected to go smoothly, but in mid-January 1994, he shocked the administration by announcing that he was withdrawing from consideration.

He lashed out at what he called a “new McCarthyism” in the news media, citing particularly what he viewed as longtime hostility and unfair criticism of him by the Times columnist William Safire, who called Admiral Inman “manipulative and deceptive” after his nomination was announced.

Admiral Inman’s relationship with the press having soured, he also said that he had heard reports that Mr. Safire and Senator Bob Dole of Kansas, the Republican minority leader, had plotted to derail his nomination, though he acknowledged he did not know whether that was true. Both Mr. Safire and Mr. Dole denied the reports.

“I did not want this job,” Mr. Inman said. “I’m at peace with myself.”

Bobby Ray Inman was born on April 4, 1931, in Rhonesboro, Texas, the second of four children of Herman and Mertie (Henson) Inman. His father owned several business, including a service station, a drugstore, a drive-in, and worked with Shell Chemical during World War II.

He went to high school in the nearby city of Mineola and graduated from the University of Texas at Austin at 19. He enlisted in the Navy in 1951, was commissioned as an ensign and served on an aircraft carrier where he was trained to decode secret messages.

In 1961, he began a 33-month stint as a military intelligence analyst at N.S.A. headquarters, keeping watch on the Soviet Navy.

“The idea of going back to be director had always been one of those wonderful dreams that appeared to be unobtainable,” he told James Bamford for his 2001 history of the N.S.A., “Body of Secrets.”

But he rose through the ranks, became the Navy intelligence chief and subsequently a vice director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, then obtained his dream job of running the N.S.A.

In addition to his son Thomas, Admiral Inman is survived by his wife, Nancy (Russo) Inman, and another son, William.

Although he had been responsible for keeping some of America’s most closely guarded secrets, Mr. Inman suggested that openness might be the best course for the N.S.A. after Edward J. Snowden, a former contractor, released a stream of the agency’s documents in 2013.

“My advice would be to take everything you think Snowden has and get it out yourself,” he told The Times. “It would certainly be a shock to the agency. But bad news doesn’t get better with age. The sooner they get it out and put it behind them, the faster they can begin to rebuild.”

Ama Sarpomaa and Gabriella DePinho contributed reporting.

item.title: Fiona the Hippo Died After Eating a Hat. Some Want Justice.
item.description:
Her rise to fame brought joy to the internet. Now, the death of Fiona the hippopotamus is igniting another specialty of the online multitudes: rage, with a dose of vigilantism.

In the hours after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona had not survived ingesting a child’s knit hat, social media commenters activated.

They have called for investigations to be conducted, video footage to be released and, most of all, for the parents of the child whose hat ended up in the enclosure to be punished. Some want them fined or sent to prison, even as others urge equanimity.

“It’s the worst thing we do as a society online, just pile on, without all the information, and with all the judgment,” said Joy Bennett, a City Council member in nearby Mason, Ohio, who joined in the fray on Facebook.

“We want reasons, culprits, and consequences so life doesn’t feel so out of control,” Ms. Bennett wrote. “But I don’t think it’s OK to attack a total stranger for something that any of us could have been part of.”

Yet the firestorm has only gathered momentum as Fiona fans around the world try to piece together the events that led to her death.

The zoo has shared that about two weeks ago, a child visiting the exhibit tossed a hat into the air. The hat was caught by a ceiling fan and sent through a one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window, and it landed in Fiona’s holding tank.

Hippos are considered extremely dangerous animals; the zoo adheres to an industry standard called protected contact, which means zoo staff will not enter the enclosures of some animals when they are present.

At first, it was not clear when the zoo staff was notified about the hat mishap, leaving online sleuths to question if anything could have been done for Fiona sooner.

But on Friday, Michelle Curley, a spokeswoman for the zoo, told The New York Times that caretakers were alerted the same day the hat landed in the enclosure, by a guest who saw what happened. She did not comment on the calls for consequences for the family that owned the hat.

“This was an accident,” she said.

A spokeswoman for the Hamilton County prosecuting attorney declined to comment.

Kimberly Legocki, a University of San Francisco professor who studies online backlash, said that whenever the details of a tragedy are unclear, internet vigilantes tend to swoop in. She has seen many online comments by people claiming, without evidence, that they knew the age of the child and the name of the mother involved.

“Right now, there’s a gap in knowledge,” Ms. Legocki said. “What happens in these cases is that they start filling in that gap.”

On Friday, as the United States Senate adopted a resolution honoring Fiona with rare speed and unanimity, the zoo’s communications focused on the necropsy of the hippo. It revealed that the hat was lodged in the middle of her small intestine, making it impossible to reach by any medical intervention.

Craig Hoover, an executive vice president at the Association of Aquariums and Zoos, of which the Cincinnati Zoo is a member, said that the criticism floating around the internet in the wake of Fiona’s death was “unfortunate and regrettable.”

“There will be time for assessing what, if anything, we might learn from this, but right now I think the focus should really be on providing support” to the zoo, Mr. Hoover said.

The Cincinnati Zoo was also home to Harambe, a gorilla who had to be killed in order to rescue a 4-year-old boy who fell into the animal’s enclosure in 2016. The boy was hurt, but not severely. Online commenters were quick to draw a comparison between the two incidents, but Mr. Hoover warned against drawing conclusions about the zoo, saying it has been accredited since 1978 and remains, “by all accounts, a world-class zoological facility.”

Jesse Lee, a veterinarian in Columbus, was thinking about the high rates of suicide in her profession when she crafted a long Facebook response to the anger she was seeing directed at both the zoo and the parents of the child who threw the hat.

“Trying to raise children in this time of bullying, trying to practice veterinary medicine in this time of bullying — I don’t know how we as a society check ourselves so we can exhibit more empathy,” she said.

At the zoo on Friday, a statue of Fiona was covered in flowers, stuffed animals and two of her favorite foods: watermelons and pumpkins. The typically bustling sidewalk, adorned with faux hippo footprints, was empty. A barrier kept onlookers away from Hippo Cove, which remained closed. Outside the zoo, a 5-year-old boy explored, watched closely by his mother, Heather Willins.

She said she felt for the parents involved but also for the people expressing their rage online.

“We will never feel closure,” Ms. Willins said. “Blaming others is part of the grieving process.”

item.title: It’s a Bill on Energy Permits, but Trump’s Pet Projects Are Part of the Debate
item.description:
Cheered on by the Trump administration, lawmakers are moving toward passing a sweeping overhaul of permitting intended to speed up construction of power plants, gas pipelines and other energy projects.

The measure is that increasingly rare species of major legislation with at least some bipartisan support, as backers argue that it could lower energy bills and unleash a wave of new projects in a country they say has made it too hard to build. But as with much in Washington, the bill is also brushing up against the pet projects and mercurial nature of President Trump.

As the legislation advances from the Senate to the House, opponents are warning that its broad implications could accelerate a range of construction projects, including Mr. Trump’s prized triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and a new championship-level golf course in Washington.

“In several of the pending lawsuits there are court orders enjoining parts of Trump’s vanity projects,” said Representative Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, who opposes the bill. “If this legislation were to become law as written, that relief might not exist.”

Chief among the opponents’ concerns: The bill essentially renders toothless both the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to assess the environmental effects of proposed actions, and the National Historic Preservation Act, which establishes a review process to try to prevent historic sites’ destruction or alteration by federal projects.

Provisions in the bill would prevent judges from halting projects for violating those laws, even ones that have nothing to do with energy production. Courts could still block projects that are found to have violated other federal laws and inflict an “irreparable harm to the plaintiff.”

Opponents of Mr. Trump’s arch and golf course have cited those two laws, among others, in their suits.

“There is still going to be a mighty effort to stop them,” Mr. Huffman said of Mr. Trump’s Washington projects. “But NEPA, injunctive relief and the National Historic Preservation Act are critical tools to stopping many of these vanity projects. As written, this bill wipes those tools away.”

Mr. Trump has indicated he would sign the legislation, and praised its provisions on Friday, calling it “one of the biggest things that you’ll see.”

But he has also railed against parts of the nearly 500-page bill. The president recently said he did not like that it could be used to speed up the construction of windmills.

“I will not approve wind turbines,” Mr. Trump said earlier this month, adding: “The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Still, his administration has been working with lawmakers on the bill, and promotes many of its provisions. As more energy projects come online, the cost of energy should drop, administration officials say. One study estimated that the bill would reduce household electricity bills by up to $78 per year by 2040.

The Senate approved the bill on Thursday, 62 to 33. All but two Republican senators voted for the bill, which had the enthusiastic support of business groups, energy developers and labor unions. Democrats were more closely split, though most voted against it. Its fate in the House is less certain.

“It’s going to cause tremendous amounts of new building,” Mr. Trump said on Friday.

Vice President JD Vance called the bill “an amazing bipartisan piece of legislation that will allow the United States to build like we’ve never built before,” acknowledging that the loosening of regulations would reach beyond energy projects.

“That means more homes, more factories, more power plants,” he said.

The bill was the result of negotiations between top Republicans and Democrats on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Republicans pushed for language that could make it harder for environmental groups to sue to block natural gas pipelines, oil drilling, mines and other energy projects. Democrats sought to make it easier to build large power lines, which could greatly expand the use of wind and solar energy.

The bill has generated objections from tribal nations and historic preservationists in addition to some environmentalists.

In a letter to the top Democrat in the House, the founding partner of Cultural Heritage Partners, Greg Werkheiser, laid out what he said were 10 terrible consequences of the bill, including eliminating the public comment process for projects affecting historic sites and no longer requiring agencies to consider visual or auditory effects of new development on historic sites unless they directly diminished the property.

“Under this new bill, which has passed the Senate, if you want to put a Walmart literally right next door to Gettysburg Battlefield, you can do it,” he said in an interview.

A spokeswoman for Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and one of the bill’s main authors, did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement issued after the Senate passed the bill, Mr. Whitehouse promoted its bolstering of clean energy.

“Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit,” he said.

item.title: F.B.I. Is Still Looking for Evidence That Georgia’s 2020 Election Was Rigged
item.description:
Federal investigators on Friday interviewed the local official in Fulton County, Ga., who oversaw vote counting in the 2020 presidential race, the latest indication that the government continues to criminally investigate an election that President Trump has repeatedly claimed without evidence was rigged.

The official, Richard Barron, the former elections director in the county, said he was interviewed on Friday afternoon in Atlanta. In attendance were two F.B.I. agents and two federal prosecutors, including Dan Bishop, a former congressman from North Carolina and Trump loyalist who was appointed in April as the Justice Department’s top election fraud prosecutor, Mr. Barron said.

The interview came 10 months after federal officials raided a government election center in Fulton County, the state’s largest jurisdiction, seizing ballots from the 2020 election and escalating an investigation driven largely by Mr. Trump’s baseless claim that his 2020 defeat in Georgia had been marred by widespread fraud.

The raid in January relied on debunked claims, according to court filings at the time, and Mr. Barron said his interview on Friday also centered around some of those claims.

In the interview, which lasted more than two hours, Mr. Barron said Mr. Bishop brought up theories about the election that have been promulgated by a number of well-known “election integrity” activists, including Garland Favorito, a Georgia resident who has for years advanced unfounded claims of fraud in the 2020 election.

At one point, Mr. Barron said, Mr. Bishop asked him if any of these theories were “reasonable.”

Mr. Barron replied that they were not.

Mr. Barron agreed to sit for an interview with his lawyer present after an F.B.I. agent approached him last week. He said that he did not receive a subpoena and had chosen to cooperate with F.B.I. agents of his own volition.

“I know that I didn’t commit a crime,” said Mr. Barron, who resigned from his county job in 2022. “And I would say, I’m 100 percent confident, that neither did any of my staff.”

The Trump administration’s ongoing interest in the six-year-old election in Fulton County has struck many observers as both unnerving and bizarre. Mr. Trump narrowly lost Georgia in 2020, and the vote was subject to multiple recounts. After the election, Mr. Trump and his allies made numerous bogus claims about election fraud in Fulton County, which covers most of Atlanta and is a Democratic stronghold.

The state of the investigation remains unclear. Neither Justice Department nor F.B.I. officials responded to requests for comment for this article, and Mr. Bishop did not return a phone call seeking comment on Friday.

Court records around the time of the January raid show that the federal government was looking for possible violations of a federal law against destruction of election-related records. The court records also cited a statute making it a crime to knowingly procure fraudulent voter registration or fraudulent votes.

No widespread evidence of such violations in 2020 has ever surfaced.

David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department, said he could not imagine there was very much left to investigate in late 2026.

“The 2020 election was the most scrutinized in world history, and Fulton County was perhaps more scrutinized than any other place in the country,” said Mr. Becker, who runs the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to support election officials.

At least two other Fulton County officials who worked on the November 2020 election have also been contacted by the F.B.I. in recent days. They include Nadine Williams, the current head of the county’s elections division, who held a management position in the office during the 2020 vote. Ms. Williams could not be reached for comment.

Federal agents have also contacted Ralph Jones, according to Morgan Elizabeth Hopkins, a family friend of his. Mr. Jones served as Fulton’s voter registration chief for over 12 years before resigning in August 2021 amid political pressure, threats and criticism of the county’s handling of the 2020 election.

Mr. Jones was at a vote-counting location at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena on Election Day in 2020 as the tally stretched past midnight. A number of Trump allies made false claims about elections workers in the arena manipulating the vote. All of those claims, including one that a mother-daughter team of election workers had dumped ballots into counting machines from suitcases, have been debunked. The two women later won a defamation suit against Rudolph W. Giuliani, one of Mr. Trump’s loudest amplifiers that year.

In the interview on Friday, Mr. Barron said that Mr. Bishop had asked him about a number of technical issues related to elections, involving what Mr. Bishop said were missing digital scans of paper ballots and other discrepancies in election record-keeping.

These issues amounted to “minor human errors seen in any election in any county across the country,” Mr. Barron said.

“It seemed like they’re trying to nitpick some way to nail somebody on a record-keeping error,” Mr. Barron said. “What it seemed to me today is that they are relying on some information that they obtained from election deniers, and that they’re using this on trivial matters that would have no impact on the election results.”

Mr. Trump and several of his allies were criminally indicted by a Fulton County grand jury in August 2023 for their efforts to overturn Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory in Georgia. The case was eventually dismissed after revelations that the district attorney, Fani T. Willis, had engaged in a romantic relationship with the lawyer she had hired to oversee it.

One key element of the prosecutors’ case was Mr. Trump’s phone call in January 2021 to Brad Raffensperger, Georgia’s secretary of state, in which the president made unfounded claims about voting irregularities that he claimed had occurred in Georgia, particularly in Fulton County.

Mr. Trump’s allegations were proven false, including an assertion that “a couple of hundred thousand forged signatures” had been signed on Fulton County’s mail-in ballots. More broadly, the bumper crop of conspiracy theories that sprang up after the 2020 election — some of them involving fantastical, science-fiction-style plots featuring space lasers and Venezuela-led voting-machine hacks — have been debunked by officials from both political parties, members of Congress, judges and law enforcement.

Nonetheless, F.B.I. agents in January descended on a hangar-like Fulton County elections facility and seized more than 600 boxes of ballots and other materials.

An unsealed affidavit that was used to obtain the search warrant for that raid relied heavily on debunked claims about ballot anomalies in 2020. The affidavit was signed by Hugh Raymond Evans, an agent with the F.B.I.’s Atlanta field office. Mr. Barron said Evans was present at the interview on Friday.

Robb Pitts, the chairman of the Fulton County Board of Commissioners, said this week he was unaware of anyone in the county receiving federal subpoenas.

“I personally have not been contacted, but I remain confident in the fact that our elections were secure and they were fair,” said Mr. Pitts, a Democrat. “Anything that the folks who were contacted will say will continue to support that, I’m sure.”

In February, Mr. Pitts filed a civil lawsuit demanding that the federal government return the seized ballots, suggesting that the move was an effort by the Trump administration to “take over” American elections.

A federal judge denied the request in May. The Justice Department also issued a subpoena demanding the identities of every worker who staffed the 2020 election in Fulton, but the county was able to quash the demand in court.

In an appearance on Fox News in April, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, said the bureau officials “have the information that backs President Trump’s claim” that the 2020 race was rigged. But Mr. Patel said he could not release information from an ongoing investigation.

The Fulton County ballot seizure sent ripples of concern through election officials across the country in the run-up to the midterms. Those fears were exacerbated by a statement Mr. Trump gave to New York Times reporters in January expressing regret for not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines in swing states after 2020.

In the weeks before this year’s midterms, a number of election and law enforcement officials discussed what to do if federal officials seized ballots or elections equipment. One such meeting took place in the Atlanta area in mid-October, according to two officials who were aware of the meeting and requested anonymity to describe it.

In July, The Times obtained an internal memo that showed that the F.B.I. had assigned 260 investigative analysts to perform hundreds of “records checks” as part of a “priority” investigation into the 2020 election in Fulton. Thus far, no criminal charges have resulted from the raid.

But the effort has come at a cost to people like Mr. Barron. He said he endured years of death threats and hateful messages as Mr. Trump and his allies spread false claims of election fraud, seizing on routine mishaps — including an overflowing urinal at the county’s ballot-counting center at State Farm Arena — to cast suspicion on the results.

“They basically chose Fulton County as their boogeyman,” he said. “It was a couple of years of hell, really.”

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

item.title: Takeaways From Trump’s Post-Asia Trip News Conference
item.description:
President Trump used a wide-ranging news conference Friday to emphasize the praise and pageantry extended to him during a trip through Asia this week, casting the beginning of his lame-duck period as president in glowing terms.

The president promoted his swing through the Philippines and China and his meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir V. Putin as major achievements, though their sessions produced no breakthroughs on crucial issues such as nuclear control, the war in Ukraine or artificial intelligence.

Mr. Trump, who did not hold a news conference after his trilateral summit in Shenzhen, spoke adoringly of the way he was treated abroad, praising the “immaculate” city that hosted him in China as pothole free. He called the relationship with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin “fantastic” and said the meeting had great “electricity.” And he sought to assure the American public that he was enjoying all of the diplomatic doting on their behalf.

“It was an amazing event. I mean, it was really amazing,” he said. “It was an honor to be representing you at that. I think we represented you very well. My whole group represented you very well.”

The president also boasted that the two leaders were impressed with his new Air Force One, a gift from Qatar, which apparently made the longest journey in the executive aircraft’s history when it flew nonstop from China to Washington on Thursday.

“It’s an amazing plane, and China was very impressed, and Russia was very impressed, and I’m very impressed,” Mr. Trump said.

After a bruising outcome in the midterms for the Republican Party and several days abroad, Mr. Trump appeared to relish the attention back at the White House. He praised the reporters, telling them that he appreciated the “turnout” in the jam-packed briefing room, which he guessed had “record” attendance. He then invited them to a musical performance and hors d’oeuvres at an event honoring the U.S. Marine Band on the new helipad he had built on the South Lawn of the White House.

Here are some takeaways from Mr. Trump’s news conference:

Mr. Trump said Nvidia’s Jensen Huang came up in his meeting with Mr. Xi, though he provided no details of what the two men said. Yet he reiterated that he would like to see Mr. Huang reinstated to his role at Nvidia.

Mr. Huang resigned from his post after revelations in The New York Times that U.S. officials concluded that he had a relationship with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset, and he also had an affair with a subordinate.

Mr. Trump said that Nvidia had put the United States ahead of China by 10 years, and that it was in the interest of the country to protect its “brilliant people.”

“I did discuss that with President Xi,” Trump said. “And he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant.’ He’s a brilliant man. He is. And I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.”

Mr. Trump threatened to bar American technology companies from building data centers outside the United States, suggesting that he could impose a “tremendous tax” on business that did so.

The president indicated that this was a recent development, noting that he had not even shared the plan with his team.

Despite growing calls to slow down A.I. advancement and data center development, Mr. Trump has reiterated that he has no intention of wavering in his support for the computing facilities, which he called “tremendous assets.”

“We’re going to fight very hard for the data centers,” Mr. Trump said, adding that he wanted the U.S. to stay ahead of China in the A.I. race.

On Monday, ahead of the president’s trip to Asia, the administration issued a rule aimed at restricting the ability of Chinese companies to gain access to data centers around the world.

Mr. Trump said that he has confidence in his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, who has recently clashed with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over his handling of a Singaporean company at the heart of revelations about Chinese spying on Nvidia.

He added that Mr. Bessent, who was in the audience, is out of “central casting” and asked him to stand up for recognition. (He did not stand, he waved instead.)

“I have not lost confidence,” he said of Mr. Lutnick. “He’s a different kind of a guy, a very good businessman. He’s not traditional like Scott is much more traditional.”

Mr. Trump said that he fired his top cybersecurity official on Thursday “because I didn’t think that person was good enough.” Sean Cairncross, who was an ally of recently ousted chief of staff Susie Wiles, was pushed out of his role after a series of technological outages affected U.S. companies and federal agencies.

Mr. Trump signaled optimism about working with Democrats on issues like health care and making it easier to produce television shows and movies in the United States.

“We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans,” he said, describing Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer — two leaders he has repeatedly attacked and insulted over the years — as smart leaders.

“There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care,” he said. “I’m open to great health care. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great health care in our country.”

He called Mr. Jeffries “a smart guy,” and a “streetwise guy.”

On immigration, Mr. Trump once again signaled possible negotiations on protections for people who have lived in the country illegally, who are “very hard-working people.” But he said he would continue focusing on deporting criminals.

Mr. Trump said he recently had a phone call with the governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, who is a Democrat. “She was really nice,” he said. “It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border.”

Mr. Trump said that during his bilateral meeting with Mr. Putin, he “clearly expressed his desire to see the war between Russia and Ukraine end by diplomatic means.” However, he did not address the fact that Russia carried out huge airstrikes against Ukraine not 24 hours later.

Mr. Trump repeated his assertion that the war would never have started if he had won the presidential election in 2020.

He claimed the Russian leader agreed with him. “I actually asked him. I said, ‘Would you have gone in if I was president?’ He said, ‘No, would have never happened.’”

When asked if Mr. Putin, who Mr. Trump has repeatedly called a “friend” of his, was a friend of America, Mr. Trump could not say.

“I can’t speak to America,” the president of the United States said.

Mr. Trump sidestepped a question about whether Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who were both standing behind him — would make a better president after he left office.

“Oh, let me give you the answer to that,” said Mr. Trump, who has publicly and privately mused about that question.

But after the newly appointed White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, gave an impassioned defense of Mr. Trump’s first two years in office, the president joked that maybe neither Mr. Vance nor Mr. Rubio would get his endorsement.

“We have breaking news,” Mr. Trump said, referring to Mr. Miller. “He was better than these two guys. Do you want to run for president?”

Reporting was contributed by Shawn McCreesh, Tony Romm, Ana Swanson, Alan Rappeport, Julian E. Barnes and Michael Crowley.

item.title: Washington State Fines Company $9 Million Over Fatal Tank Implosion
item.description:
Regulators in Washington State say executives and managers of the global paper company Nippon Dynawave Packaging knew that conditions at its plant in Longview, Wash., were unsafe months before a chemical tank implosion that killed 11 workers.

On Friday, the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries fined Nippon Dynawave, a subsidiary of a Tokyo-based company, more than $9 million, citing 75 workplace safety violations. Investigators planned to send their findings to criminal prosecutors, asserting that the company’s inaction was “both willful and contributed directly to the deaths of their workers.”

Joel Sacks, director of the state labor department, said the report was “shocking and heartbreaking.”

“Nippon Dynawave had all the information they needed to act, but they didn’t listen to alarms their consultants and staff were raising,” he said.

In a written statement, the company said it had cooperated with investigators and that the state report had “failed to include important facts and context.” The company plans to appeal the fine and the ruling, it said.

On May 26, a tank holding a toxic mix of chemicals used to break down wood into pulp failed at the plant, about an hour north of Portland, Ore., on the Columbia River. Almost 900,000 gallons of “white liquor” heated to 200 degrees flooded into a surrounding courtyard and nearby buildings.

The 11 workers who died all suffered severe chemical burns. One also suffered blunt-force injuries and another died partly from asphyxia. At least nine other people were injured.

During a six-month investigation, state regulators found that a July 2025 inspection showed that the walls of the tank were too thin and documented a series of exchanges between company officials about the problem. According to the state report, the inspector predicted a “high likelihood” that the tank would fail.

Factory employees debated removing the tank from service, according to emails state investigators obtained. More tests confirmed that the tank no longer met minimum safety standards. Officials at the Longview plant asked the company to include a replacement tank in its 2026 capital budget but were told “that they will have to reduce capital expenses before adding” a replacement tank to the budget. State investigators say managers at the local plant “chose to prioritize other projects.”

It’s not clear from the state report why officials at the Longview plant or Nippon Dynawave’s corporate offices kept the aging tank in service, despite three separate reports showing that the walls of the tank were corroded beyond acceptable or safe levels. The state findings echo a preliminary report by federal chemical safety inspectors issued in August.

Investigators said the company had failed to conduct regular internal inspections on 14 tanks at the Longview plant, including the one that failed.

item.title: A Prosecutor Got Drunk to Help the Police. Things Got Out of Hand.
item.description:
The assignment was straightforward enough, if a little odd, given that it took place in a room full of police officers: Get drunk.

And that was precisely what the young prosecutor did — arguably too well.

So well that his boss, of all people, announced in a statement this week that he had “achieved a high B.A.C.” — blood alcohol content — “and, unfortunately, did not conduct himself in a professional way.”

The prosecutor, a recent hire at the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office in Arizona, had been participating last month in a “controlled alcohol workshop,” a type of training designed to help law enforcement agents learn how to detect inebriation by having them watch other attendees imbibe. Also known as a wet lab, it is a longstanding practice that, officials say, helps them crack down on drunk driving.

But in this case, what was supposed to be a strictly controlled seminar apparently got out of hand. The prosecutor, who was not identified by the county attorney’s office, clocked a blood alcohol level of 0.247, much higher than the 0.15 maximum for such trainings set by state policy and beyond what Arizona law considers to be “extreme” intoxication.

What happened next might have been predictable.

“He exhibited poor judgment by running out of the building and acting in an argumentative manner,” Rachel Mitchell, the Maricopa County attorney, said in a statement on Thursday. “He was driven home and apologized that same evening for his conduct.”

There was no evidence that the prosecutor broke any laws, she said.

The incident, which took place on a Friday night in Queen Creek, a fast-growing suburb southeast of Phoenix, led to an internal investigation and disciplinary action, Ms. Mitchell said. She did not specify how the prosecutor was reprimanded but said he would not be allowed to participate in other wet labs.

The Queen Creek Police Department, which conducted the training, said in a statement on Friday evening that the prosecutor’s behavior did not warrant a criminal investigation, but the department did not explain why he was allowed to continue drinking beyond the prescribed amount.

J.M. Torrez, the director of the Arizona Governor’s Office of Highway Safety, which funds and oversees wet lab trainings statewide, said he and other officials were reviewing the episode to ensure future sessions do not go similarly sideways. Over the last decade, agencies across the state have conducted 166 wet labs, Mr. Torrez said, and he was not aware of another such incident.

“This is a great learning moment,” Mr. Torrez said. “Alcohol impairs your judgment. The moment you consume alcohol, your judgment starts to go. That’s why everybody loves karaoke in a bar, because they all think they’re Frank Sinatra.”

Typical wet labs involve volunteers who sign consent waivers and drink measured quantities of alcohol while their B.A.C. is monitored. Instructors are supposed to keep a close watch throughout the exercise. Trainees then administer a battery of tests to the tipsy participants, tracking their eye movement, having them walk in a straight line and asking them to stand on one leg.

In this case, there was clearly a failure to control the prosecutor’s alcohol intake, Mr. Torrez said. But other policies that were in place, such as ensuring all volunteers are driven home, he said, meant “nothing criminal occurred, nothing catastrophic occurred.”

Wet labs are critical, especially for early-career officers, Mr. Torrez said. They allow them to practice field sobriety tests in a controlled setting, rather than perform them for the first time during a traffic stop on a busy roadside with cars speeding past, he said.

Christian Lueders, a former Maricopa County prosecutor, said his former colleagues saw the trainings as a chance to take part in some “state-sanctioned drinking.” He said he never participated but heard they were always “a friendly, fun environment.”

For police officers, the training is valuable, said Mr. Lueders, who is now a criminal defense attorney. But in this case, he said, “It does seem a little bit reckless that they would let someone get to that level.”

Julie Gunnigle, a public interest lawyer and a former Democratic nominee for Maricopa County attorney, said the wet lab misadventure highlighted a troubling practice. She recalled that when she was a young attorney working in Indiana, such trainings were seen as perks, even if they could lead to disorderly conduct.

“They were an open invitation to have a few beers on the government’s dime,” said Ms. Gunnigle, who added that she never took part herself. “The hypocrisy is not lost on me that the very same behavior from a civilian could land them with a misdemeanor charge.”

item.title: Federal Court Halts Pregnant Workers’ Protection Law
item.description:
A federal court ruled Friday night that a landmark pandemic-era law that requires employers to provide on-the-job accommodations to pregnant women passed with proxy voters in violation of the Constitution.

Legal experts said the decision would effectively invalidate the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, home to about 20 million women, and would likely have ripple effects nationally.

The law protects accommodations for pregnant workers such as bathroom and water breaks, relief from heavy lifting and time off for prenatal appointments. The decisionis expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 9 to 8 that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was passed by Congress in violation of the Constitution’s quorum clause, which requires a majority of members in each chamber of Congress to be present to conduct official business.

The law was passed as part of a broader $1.7 trillion spending bill during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic, as lawmakers authorized remote and proxy votes as a safety precaution.

“We conclude that the Act’s passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum,” the judges wrote, saying that the proxy system established during the pandemic was at odds with the standards established by the framers of the Constitution. “At the Constitutional Convention, the Framers vigorously debated a quorum threshold for Congress to conduct business,” the judges wrote. “Indeed, early legislatures never attempted to ameliorate such concerns via proxies, even though the Founding generation was surely aware of the existence of that device.”

The court’s decision was a victory for outgoing Texas attorney general Ken Paxton, who had brought the suit on behalf of the state as an employer.

The suit said that the law “purports to subject [the state] to the costs, hassles, and attendant risks of administrative proceedings, investigations, and lawsuits, by both private individuals and the federal government.”

The decision immediately ends the requirement for the state of Texas, as an employer, to enforce the pregnant workers’ law. It also means, legal experts said, that any other employer in the jurisdiction of the Fifth Circuit that was challenged to enforce the law could assume that they would prevail in such a challenge.

The law has drawn opposition from employers as pregnant workers have used it to demand on-the-job protections. A Texas accountant won $376,000 in damages in a court decision this year maintaining that her employer had violated the law by refusing to allow her to work remotely while pregnant. Warehouse workers have used the law as the basis of a class-action lawsuit claiming that Amazon denied accommodations to thousands of pregnant employees.

Women’s rights advocates and experts in constitutional law said the implications of halting enforcement of the law could be profound.

“This decision effectively erases essential rights to pregnancy accommodations for workers across Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi,” said Inimai Chettiar, president of A Better Balance, a women’s legal advocacy group that wrote an amicus brief in favor of upholding the law. “The Fifth Circuit has put the health, livelihoods, and economic security of millions of American women and their families at risk.”

The decision “will have dramatic and destructive real-world consequences,” said William Eskridge, a scholar of constitutional law at Yale University.

Mr. Eskridge and other legal experts said it was highly unusual for the court to declare Congress’s use of proxy and remote voting during the Covid pandemic to be unconstitutional.

“It’s breaking down the separation of powers if the courts get to second-guess the choices that the House made about its own rules in terms of how it was going to count votes,” said Deborah Widiss, a professor of law at Indiana University Bloomington.

Even Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, formerly a Senate Republican leader, filed an amicus brief in favor of upholding the law. “The core question in this case is whether the courts can review the internal affairs of Congress, when such affairs are textually committed to each house by the Constitution,” he wrote. “They cannot.”

Experts also pointed out that the decision now throws into legal question the status of the $1.7 trillion spending bill that had been the legislative vehicle for passage of the pregnant workers’ act.

That bill also included about $858 billion in defense spending, including $436 million for military facilities in Texas.

While the judges’ decision halted only enforcement of the pregnant workers’ provisions, the dissenting judges wrote, “There is no explanation offered to explain why, if the entirety of the statute was unconstitutionally passed, this court’s judgment should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill.”

Ms. Widiss, the law professor, said the decision opens the door to legal challenges to the other spending, which could potentially also be considered unconstitutional. She said, “If the Fifth Circuit’s constitutional reasoning is correct, then the whole bill and the entire $1.7 trillion that it authorized was passed improperly.”

item.title: A Punk Rocker’s Painful Wait for Wheelchair Repairs
item.description:
Even before a car crash left him paralyzed, Will Good and the rest of the Old Edison hadn’t performed much in years. The band used to be a regular part of the Boston band scene, hollering folk punk over the twanging of a banjo and fiddle.

Almost six years ago, the crash left Mr. Good hospitalized with a spinal cord injury. As he recovered, well-wishers brought records to add to his vinyl collection. They sat on his shelf, unplayed. Mr. Good had stopped listening to music, and wouldn’t again for a long time.

“It was a huge part of my life, and I didn’t know how to have a relationship with it,” he said.

This summer, the Old Edison encouraged Mr. Good to play a reunion show. Now 36, he would be behind the microphone again, belting out the band’s songs from his motorized wheelchair.

A month before the performance, his specialized chair broke down.

He quickly found himself in a painful limbo that has become increasingly common for many types of wheelchair users across the country. With many local repair shops being bought out by two national companies, the wait for wheelchair repairs can now stretch into weeks, or months, leading to dangerous health complications.

“I’m losing my mind,” Mr. Good said nine days before showtime. Without use of his chair, he spent most of the month leading up to the reunion performance bedridden, dealing with near-constant pain.

More than five million people in the United States use wheelchairs. Some require complex personalization to accommodate particular injuries or disabilities. When those chairs break down, users can find themselves housebound or bedridden, unable to go to work, to school or to medical appointments.

Wait times for service have ballooned over the last decade. Lengthy health insurance approvals and slow parts shipments play a role in the growing backlog. But the delays also corresponded with two private equity-backed companies devouring smaller competitors.

Numotion and National Seating & Mobility now dominate the U.S. market, according to experts, and have greater reach in some states. For instance, Numotion had 47 percent of the Connecticut market and National Seating & Mobility had 45 percent based on revenue, according to a 2024 report to the Connecticut legislature.

“Private equity entering the space has been dangerous,” said Lynn Worobey, who studies wheelchair use at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. “It used to be a lot of smaller, kind of mom-and-pop stores that were doing this,” she added, “and they have been kind of scooped up by these larger firms.”

Numotion has acquired at least 25 competitors since it was formed in 2013, out of a merger between two smaller companies, according to a report by disability rights advocates and private equity trackers. National Seating & Mobility has bought up at least 42 other companies since 2013, according to the report.

AEA Investors acquired Numotion in 2018. National Seating & Mobility is now owned by Cinven. Both are private equity firms.

Industry representatives declined to comment on specific market data, though Numotion’s website says the company serves more than half a million wheelchair users. A company spokeswoman, Andrea Barnett, acknowledged in a statement that delays are a serious problem and said her company is working on solutions.

It can be difficult to repair highly personalized health equipment and the process is slowed by many outside factors, said Wayne Grau, executive director at the National Coalition For Assistive & Rehab Technology, an industry trade group. National Seating & Mobility would not comment, but said the company supported Mr. Grau’s statement.

The repair delays have prompted investigations by regulators, lawmakers and the news media, including Mother Jones and NPR. California, Colorado, Maryland, Nevada, Oregon and Washington have enacted wheelchair right-to-repair laws over the past five years.

Connecticut now requires companies to complete repairs within 10 business days, and Massachusetts lawmakers have introduced a similar bill.

Chairs like the one Mr. Good relies on are customized, and often do more than wheel a person from place to place. Mr. Good’s, for example, tilts back so that he can relieve the pressure on his skin. A friend’s loaner that he used in the month before his reunion show didn’t fit him right, causing constant pain. He strained to drive it, and kept slipping out.

As a result, he spent most of his time in bed, agonizing over whether his own chair would be fixed before the performance.

The specialized chairs can cost tens of thousands of dollars, yet they frequently break down. Two surveys, including one of veterans and another of users with spinal cord injuries, indicated that more than half needed repairs over a six-month period.

Long waits can lead to life-threatening problems.

While waiting for his repair, Mr. Good developed a pressure wound, caused by the loss of blood flow and breakdown of tissue. About 60,000 hospital patients die from such injuries each year, according to the Department for Health and Human Services.

In July, four days before his reunion show, Mr. Good spent the afternoon waiting for a message from a repair technician as he sat home by his record collection.

Music has turned from a source of pain to once again provide comfort. Mr. Good said he is listening lately to post-punk emo and the new Busta Rhymes record. He has been to several shows, including a Noah Kahan concert at Fenway Park and a Dropkick Murphys show opened by Haywire, the Boston hardcore punk band.

“I need that connectivity,” Mr. Good said. “I need the outlet. I need the community. I need the reprieve.”

That afternoon in July, a past experience had Mr. Good worried that something would go wrong during his repair appointment. Several years ago, a repairman had shown up with a replacement foot plate for the wrong side of the chair.

So when the technician arrived with a tool kit and a cardboard box and saying there had been a problem, Mr. Good was ready to erupt in fury.

The manufacturer had sent the wrong computer part. But the technician said he had managed to swap it for the right one. After a three-and-a-half week wait, the repair took about 15 minutes.

“I’m so lucky,” Mr. Good repeated afterward. “I’m so lucky.”

A few days later, as planned, the Old Edison performed a Sunday matinee for a crowd that had grown up in Boston’s punk scene. As the band altered some of its songs to fit Mr. Good’s slower pace and new vocal range, the crowd still shook fists in the air and belted out the lyrics along with him.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: International Student Enrollment Plunged. Schools Are Bracing for More Losses.
item.description:
The Trump administration’s crackdown on international students is deepening, as it moves to impose new rules and fees that higher education leaders say are likely to further cut enrollment from abroad, which has already dropped by 15 percent this fall.

The recent actions targeting the roughly 1.1 million international students in the United States would make it harder for them to work in the country and, critics say, discourage them from enrolling in American schools.

Universities have pushed back against a federal proposal last month to charge at least $70,000 for student visa holders to gain access to a popular program that lets them work temporarily in the United States after graduation. The administration would charge an extra $30,000 for STEM graduates to receive extensions in the program, known as Optional Practical Training.

The fees would be charged to colleges and universities, and if that cost is passed to students, many fewer could come to the United States.

“In the beginning of the administration, they were taking a hammer to everything and really shocking the system,” said Daniel Delgado, a former senior Department of Homeland Security official who now works at the Searchlight Institute, a centrist Democratic think tank. “Now we’re seeing them translate that into policy.”

The Trump administration has aggressively targeted international students as part of its broader campaign to restrict immigration, arguing that curbing their enrollment would prevent companies from sidelining Americans, especially amid layoffs in the tech industry.

But the recent actions have drawn sharp criticism from universities and business groups that say the loss of international students would make it harder for companies to hire top talent, hurting the country’s competitiveness. Tech leaders have long said that there are not enough U.S. workers for all of their specialized roles, and that international students help fill those gaps.

.

Dennis Galvan, the vice provost for global engagement at the University of Oregon, said the fee would likely have an “even bigger negative effect” on enrollment. The number of international students at the university had already dropped by about 14 percent compared with 2024, he said.

The Optional Practical Training program is “one of the biggest draws” for foreign students to come to the United States and study at the university, Mr. Galvan said. But the university probably would not be able to cover the program’s costs if the fee was imposed, he said.

Many international students rely on the program before seeking H-1B visas, a small number of which are granted to skilled foreign workers each year. Trump officials have also taken aim at the H-1B program, which they have accused of undercutting Americans.

In August, the administration proposed attaching a steep $103,265 fee for H-1B visas, echoing a move by the president last year that was blocked by the courts. This time, the administration is trying to formalize the fee by using a different legal process.

In September, federal officials proposed ending the 60-day grace period that H-1B and other visa holders have to remain in the country after losing their jobs, essentially making them subject to deportation immediately.

The administration’s efforts are expected to face legal challenges. Some of its policies have already been blocked. On Monday, a federal judge vacated a rule that sought to limit the period that students can remain in the country, an attempt to reverse a policy known as duration of status.

The Department of Homeland Security said the proposals would help protect U.S. workers and the country’s “national identity.”

“Our immigration system is being reformed to serve American citizens, American workers, American families, and preserve our national identity, not rapidly import foreigners who take American jobs, commit crimes, burden our welfare system and erode our cultural and social fabric,” the department said in a statement.

Arizona State University was among dozens of schools that criticized the new fee, saying it could “severely damage international enrollment.” That could even affect students from the United States, the university said, because international students often pay full tuition. Losing them, it added, would weaken its “financial base” and academic programs.

Some students worry that if schools pass on the costs of the new fee to them, they would be unable to pursue work in the United States.

Sandra Ding, a senior at the University of California, Berkeley who came to the school from China, said she could not afford to pay at least $70,000 for work authorization.

“Affording an education here is already a huge burden on my family,” said Ms. Ding, who is studying psychology and cognitive science.

The attempts to overhaul work authorization programs are resurfacing tensions with business groups that have at times clashed with the administration over its immigration agenda. In public comments this month, the Chamber of Commerce and organizations representing tech companies, including Apple and Meta, said the new policies would hurt employers and their ability to recruit workers with critical skills.

Mr. Trump has at times scaled back his restrictive immigration policies after outcry from businesses, raising questions about the future of the latest proposals. But administration officials have also made clear that they will pursue what they say is fraud in visa programs.

Miriam Feldblum, the head of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a group of university leaders, said the administration had been “flooding the zone” with policies targeting international students.

Her group sued the administration over its dismantling of the duration of status policy. The alliance has also challenged the administration’s attempts to limit the Curricular Practical Training program, which authorizes international students to complete internships and other work experiences while enrolled in school. On Tuesday, a federal judge blocked the administration, for now, from carrying out the policy.

Critics of the efforts say the loss of international students would stifle U.S. economic growth and innovation. Economists have generally found that H-1B visa holders boost American productivity, even if it has long been a source of controversy that has garnered bipartisan calls for reform.

“It’s going to have ripple effects throughout the whole economy,” said Jeremy Neufeld, the director of immigration policy at the Institute for Progress, a think tank focused on innovation.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump would continue to focus on growing the U.S. economy, and that there was “no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force.”

Proponents of the administration said they welcomed the Trump administration’s attempts to prioritize American workers.

“Absolutely it is a positive step, and I would even say long overdue,” said Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that favors lower immigration rates.

item.title: The 77-Year-Old Grandparents Accused of Killing Their Son-in-Law
item.description:
On a warm Saturday afternoon this fall, Jonathan McKinsey had just finished playing with his three children at a Bay Area park. He dragged a wagon past a baseball diamond and crowded playground and began to load items into the trunk of his SUV.

Then a bullet struck the back of his head, prosecutors say. Within 40 seconds, at least 17 more rounds were fired at Mr. McKinsey.

It was shocking enough that Mr. McKinsey was shot repeatedly in a park filled with children in Dublin, Calif., a Bay Area suburb popular among tech workers.

But the killing, on Sept. 26, reverberated far beyond Northern California after the authorities said the assailants were Mr. McKinsey’s 77-year-old in-laws. And headlines all over the world noted Mr. McKinsey’s role as director of engineering for the department at The New York Times that produces Wordle and other games.

Prosecutors say that the in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, jointly carried out a murder plot amid contentious divorce proceedings and a custody battle between Mr. McKinsey and their daughter, Candice Jang. Mr. McKinsey had been married to Ms. Jang for 15 years and had three children, with her before they were recently separated.

Defense lawyers have not disputed that the couple shot Mr. McKinsey, but say that they did so out of fear for their safety as well as the safety of their daughter and grandchildren. They cite child abuse allegations against Mr. McKinsey as well as the ongoing family court proceedings.

“The larger court record is replete with facts supporting both self-defense and defense of others,” Amy Cheng, a deputy public defender who represents Mr. Zhang, said in a recent filing.

The details of the allegations are laid out in court documents that have been unsealed or filed in recent weeks. Mr. Zhang, Ms. Chen and their lawyers could not be reached for comment. The Alameda County District Attorney’s office, which is prosecuting the case, said it would not comment on an ongoing case.

Both Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen have pleaded not guilty and are being held without bail. They are expected to return to court on Monday for a pretrial hearing.

Prosecutors say that they believe Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen planned the shooting, and the murder charge the couple faces includes a special circumstance of “lying in wait.”

Mr. Zhang typically got around by bicycle, prosecutors say, but he rented a car the day before the shooting. His wife of nearly half a century, Ms. Chen, was behind the wheel and wearing a wig as the couple drove to the park. They brought with them two loaded pistols, according to the documents.

The couple, prosecutors say, waited at the park for several minutes until Mr. McKinsey handed off the three children to their daughter, who drove off.

Then, just after 3 p.m. in the Dublin Sports Grounds parking lot, Mr. Zhang shot Mr. McKinsey once in the back of the head, causing him to fall to the ground, police say. Mr. Zhang continued to fire at him while he lay motionless, according to footage captured by a school camera across the street that was cited by prosecutors and defense lawyers.

Seconds later, Ms. Chen left the vehicle and fired a second gun several times at Mr. McKinsey, who remained on the ground, prosecutors say. Mr. Zhang fired at him again, and the couple stared down at Mr. McKinsey, prosecutors said.

After the shooting, detectives found four photo albums in the Dublin apartment where Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen live. Mr. McKinsey’s face cut out of some of the pictures. On one photo, there were black ink marks on his chest and over his right eye, the very places he was later shot, prosecutors say.

After his arrest, Mr. Zhang was interviewed by the police, through a Mandarin interpreter. According to court documents, Mr. Zhang told the police that he had been thinking about killing Mr. McKinsey all day and that he had rented the car so he could drive to a gun range and practice shooting.

Mr. Zhang, a retired metallurgist, immigrated to Albuquerque from China in 1985. He was joined three years later by his wife and daughter. In 2016, he and his wife relocated to Northern California to be closer to their daughter and her family.

Years later, at the time of the shooting, Mr. Zhang believed that Mr. McKinsey had a “dark soul” and had treated his grandchildren poorly, including physical abuse, he told the police, according to court documents. He also believed his son-in-law had wanted to harm him.

Mr. McKinsey and his wife, Ms. Jang, 46, had each accused each other of verbal, physical and psychological abuse, according to previous court records. Mr. McKinsey was a transgender man and had accused Ms. Jang and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity.

Katharine Tinto, a clinical law professor at the University of California, Irvine, said the outcome of the case could hinge on the defendants’ state of mind during the killing.

Mr. Zhang was diagnosed with memory loss last year, his lawyers said. Ms. Chen’s lawyer said that Mr. Zhang was “in the grips of serious mental deterioration” and becoming increasingly paranoid about Mr. McKinsey.

Those factors or a self-defense argument could throw into question the proof of advanced planning required for a murder conviction, Ms. Tinto said.

“That’s what the heart of this case seems to be: how culpable are these parents, and what was their intention, what was their mental state when they did these acts?” she said.

Mr. Zhang told detectives that he told his wife to drive them to the park and to bring a gun, but that she did not know anything more. They did not discuss killing Mr. McKinsey, Mr. Zhang told detectives.

Ms. Chen’s attorney, Curtis Briggs, wrote in a recent court filing that Ms. Chen could not see clearly what was happening from the driver’s seat of the car when Mr. Zhang was shooting at Mr. McKinsey. She saw what appeared to be her husband doubled over in pain clutching his abdomen, and rushed out to protect him from what she feared was an assault from a “violent and dangerous Mr. McKinsey,” Mr. Briggs said.

But prosecutors argue that Ms. Chen knew of her husband’s plan because she brought a firearm and wore a black wig to cover her normally silver hair.

It remains unclear what, if anything, Ms. Jang knew about their plans. Investigators have searched her home, but she has not been charged with a crime. She declined to be interviewed when reached by phone.

On a recorded jail-line call between Ms. Jang and Ms. Chen, Ms. Chen asked her daughter to return the rental car so that it didn’t accumulate late fees, according to Mr. Briggs’ court filings.

She told her repeatedly to take good care of the children. And, according to the filings, she apologized for “all the stress I’m causing you.”

Amy Qin contributed reporting.
